title: Three perfect days in London
dek: Agatha Christie arrives at the British Library, Korea fills the British Museum and the Thames goes dark by five. A Halloween weekend of museums, markets, a proper pub and a Sunday roast.

hero.caption: Tower Bridge, where the Thames turns from the City toward the East End.

intro:
The clocks went back last Sunday, and London has settled into its early-dark season: the sun sets at about 4:38 p.m. on Friday and a couple of minutes earlier each day after. That is not a problem in a city built for indoor afternoons. This weekend the British Library opens **Agatha Christie: A World of Mystery** on Friday 30 October, its biggest show on her writing in almost 25 years, with the 1937 Remington typewriter she used for *And Then There Were None*. Across Bloomsbury, the British Museum's **Korea** exhibition covers two thousand years of art, and the Bayeux Tapestry is on view there too, though its tickets are sold out until spring.

Saturday is Halloween. Expect costumes on the Tube and full pubs, and two big home games in London: Chelsea play Manchester United at lunchtime and Spurs play Crystal Palace in the early evening. Don't plan around fireworks, because London's big Bonfire Night displays at Alexandra Palace, Battersea Park and Blackheath are all on the following weekend, 7 and 8 November.

The plan keeps each day compact. Friday is King's Cross and Bloomsbury, with Christie, Korea, a Victorian pub and a wine-bar dinner. Saturday follows the south bank of the river from Borough Market to Tate Modern and Shakespeare's Globe. Sunday is the East End: flowers on Columbia Road, a salt beef bagel on Brick Lane, a roast on Hackney Road and the new V&A East in Stratford. The forecast is mild for the season, with sunny spells on Friday and cloud on Saturday. One catch: the Piccadilly line is closed end to end on Saturday and Sunday, so read the transport notes below before you land.

days.title: Friday: King's Cross and Bloomsbury
days.intro: Opening day for Agatha Christie at the British Library, then Korea at the British Museum, which stays open late on Fridays.

stops.name: Dishoom King's Cross
stops.text: Dishoom's King's Cross branch fills a converted Victorian goods shed off Granary Square. It opens at 8 a.m. on weekdays, and breakfast is the easiest time to get in without a long wait. Order the bacon naan roll or the eggs Kejriwal on chilli cheese toast, and let them keep refilling the chai. It's a full breakfast in a big room, and you'll need it for a long museum day. **Practical:** from here the British Library is a 10-minute walk down to the Euston Road.

stops.name: Agatha Christie: A World of Mystery, British Library
stops.text: Today is opening day. The exhibition gathers more than 100 items from the Library and the Christie Archive Trust, some never shown before, and moves through a series of settings: a country house, a First World War dispensary with her 1917 pharmacy exam notes, an Orient Express-style carriage, an archaeological dig with her Leica, and a West End theatre with notes for *Witness for the Prosecution*. Look for the Remington she used to type *And Then There Were None*. **Practical:** standard tickets are £20 and the Library opens at 9:30 a.m. Book a timed slot, since opening weekends go fast.

stops.name: Lina Stores King's Cross
stops.text: Lina Stores began as a Soho deli, and its King's Cross restaurant keeps the deli at the front, with fresh pasta as the main event at lunch and dinner. Share some antipasti, order a plate of pasta each, and leave room for a cannolo from the dessert counter. It's a quick, good lunch that keeps you near the station. **Practical:** the restaurant opens at noon. It takes bookings online, but the kitchen counter is kept for walk-ins, and it's cashless.

stops.name: Korea, British Museum
stops.text: Walk 20 minutes south through Bloomsbury's squares to the British Museum's big autumn show, upstairs in Room 35 off the Great Court. It covers two thousand years of Korean making, from Buddhist figures and celadon ewers to the six-panel *Sun, Moon and Five Peaks* screen and a folk painting of a tiger and magpie. Afterwards, the permanent galleries are free. **Practical:** adult tickets are £20 for a timed slot. On Fridays the museum stays open until 8:30 p.m., so you can take your time. The Bayeux Tapestry in Room 30 is sold out through March, but ask at the desk anyway.

stops.name: The Lamb
stops.text: By now it's dark, which suits this Grade II listed Victorian pub, with its etched-glass snob screens round the bar and an old polyphon music box. It's a Young's house that serves only cask ale, so order a Young's London Original or a St Austell Proper Job and find a corner. The pub was refurbished this summer. **Practical:** on Fridays it serves until 11:30 p.m. and food until 9 p.m. It's a 10-minute walk from the museum, and Noble Rot is a few doors along the same street.

stops.name: Noble Rot
stops.text: Noble Rot is a candlelit wine bar and restaurant run by the people behind the wine magazine of the same name, whose covers hang on the dark-wood walls. The 2026 Michelin Guide calls the cooking classical and unfussy French, and recent menus have included dishes like braised turbot in vin jaune and Swaledale mutton chops. The real reason to come is the list: ask the staff to pour you something by the glass that you wouldn't usually try. **Practical:** open Monday to Saturday from noon, closed Sundays. Book ahead for a Friday.

days.title: Saturday: Bankside on Halloween
days.intro: A walk along the south bank of the Thames: market breakfast, photographs at Tate Modern, the Globe, then a galleried inn as it gets dark.

stops.name: Monmouth Coffee
stops.text: Monmouth has been roasting in this part of south London for decades, and its Park Street shop on the edge of Borough Market is where the morning starts for many locals. Order a single-cone filter or a flat white and eat a pastry standing on the pavement with everyone else. **Practical:** it opens at 7:30 a.m. Monday to Saturday and is closed on Sundays, so today's your day. Bring a reusable cup if you want it to take away, because the shop has stopped using single-use paper cups.

stops.name: Borough Market
stops.text: Saturday is the market's longest day. It opens at 9 a.m., and the first hour is the calmest, before the crowds arrive at 11. Walk the covered halls under the railway arches and graze slowly, from cheese and charcuterie stalls to bakers and fishmongers. Buy a picnic for later, or just look, since the market is as good for wandering as it is for eating. **Practical:** open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Saturdays and closed on Mondays. Tate Modern is a 15-minute riverside walk west past Southwark Cathedral and the Golden Hinde.

stops.name: Tate Modern
stops.text: Start in the Turbine Hall, where this year's free Hyundai Commission is by the Lebanese sound artist Tarek Atoui. Then go up to Level 3 for **Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography**, the first big show to treat pictorialism, the soft-focus movement that argued photographs could be art, as a global story. It has more than 200 rare prints by over 80 photographers, including Fan Ho's *Smoky World* from Hong Kong. **Practical:** exhibition tickets are £20. The gallery is open until 9 p.m. on Saturdays, so you could come back after dark instead.

stops.name: Bar Douro
stops.text: A small Portuguese counter restaurant in a railway arch, ten minutes' walk inland from the Tate. Sit at the bar and order small plates: the octopus and the croquettes get the most praise from regulars. If you want something quicker, the bifana, a sandwich of pork shoulder poached in white wine, comes with a Super Bock on Thursdays to Sundays. Pair the rest with a glass of white port and tonic or something from the Douro Valley. **Practical:** opens at noon on Saturdays. Book a counter seat, since a Saturday lunch near the market fills up.

stops.name: Shakespeare's Globe guided tour
stops.text: The reconstructed Globe has no shows this weekend, but the guided tour takes you inside the open-air theatre and tells the story from the first 1599 playhouse to its rebuilding in the 1990s. Then you can browse the exhibition of costumes and props on your own. It's a good way to spend the last of the daylight, because sunset is at about 4:36 p.m. **Practical:** adult tickets are £31 and under-16s are £14. Allow about 90 minutes in all. The Globe is running Halloween face painting for children on 30 and 31 October.

stops.name: The George Inn
stops.text: Walk back east along the river in the dark, with St Paul's lit up across the water, to London's last galleried coaching inn. It was rebuilt in 1676 after a fire and has belonged to the National Trust since 1937. Get a pint of cask ale in the Parliament Bar, with its old woodwork and clock, and if it's quiet, look up at the wooden galleries over the courtyard. **Practical:** open until midnight on Saturdays. On Halloween night the courtyard will be loud and full, so come early to get a seat inside.

stops.name: Hawksmoor Borough
stops.text: Hawksmoor is London's best-known steakhouse group, and its Borough branch, tucked behind the market, is a good warm place to spend a dark Saturday. Order a steak from the day's cuts with chips, start with a cocktail, and keep it simple. On Halloween, when most bars are packed, a booked table is the calmest option for the night. **Practical:** the kitchen is open noon to 10 p.m. on Saturdays. Some seats are kept for walk-ins, but book for a weekend. The restaurant isn't currently wheelchair accessible.

days.title: Sunday: the East End
days.intro: Columbia Road's flower market, Brick Lane's bagels, a long roast on Hackney Road, then a new museum in Stratford.

stops.name: Beigel Bake
stops.text: Open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, the white-fronted bakery at the top of Brick Lane is an East End institution. Order the salt beef bagel, hand-carved and served hot with mustard and a pickle, or a cheaper smoked salmon and cream cheese. Eat on the pavement. It's a cheap breakfast and a good start before the flower market. **Practical:** there's often a short queue, and it moves fast. Columbia Road is a 10-minute walk north-east.

stops.name: Columbia Road Flower Market
stops.text: Every Sunday this Victorian terrace fills with plant and flower stalls, and traders call out prices that drop as the day goes on. In late autumn look for the season's cut flowers, bulbs and potted plants. The small shops behind the stalls, about 60 of them, sell vintage clothes, antiques and ceramics. **Practical:** the market runs roughly 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. on Sundays only. Before 9:30 a.m. you can still walk the street comfortably, and after that it's shoulder to shoulder.

stops.name: Museum of the Home
stops.text: Set in 18th-century almshouses on Kingsland Road, this free museum shows how Londoners have lived at home over four hundred years, through a row of rebuilt living rooms from different periods. It's small and quiet, and it gives you a sense of how ordinary people lived in this city, not just its kings and bankers. **Practical:** open Tuesday to Sunday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and free. The entrance is opposite Hoxton Overground station. The gardens closed during last weekend's high winds, so check that they've reopened.

stops.name: The Marksman
stops.text: This is the Sunday roast. The Marksman is an old East End pub with a serious kitchen, and Sunday lunch is its busiest service. Recent diners describe roast beef cooked pink, with Yorkshire pudding, roast potatoes, bread sauce, carrots and buttery greens. Take your time, because a roast and a pint is the right way to spend an early-dark Sunday afternoon in London. **Practical:** lunch runs noon to 3:30 p.m. on Sundays. Book well ahead for a table. From here, Bethnal Green station on the Central line is two stops from Stratford.

stops.name: V&A East Museum
stops.text: London's newest major museum opened in April on the Olympic Park waterfront. The free *Why We Make* galleries hold more than 500 objects from the V&A collection, and the ticketed exhibition **The Music is Black: A British Story** follows 125 years of Black British music through more than 200 objects, including Winifred Atwell's piano and Joan Armatrading's childhood guitar. It's a fresh way to end a weekend of old London. **Practical:** open until 6 p.m. on Sundays. Allow 15 to 20 minutes to walk from Stratford station. Book the exhibition ahead.

stay.name: The Ned
stay.text: Edwin Lutyens designed this building as the Midland Bank's headquarters in the 1920s, and it has been a hotel since 2017. The old banking hall is now a row of restaurants and bars with live music, and the vault is a cocktail lounge behind a 20-ton door. It sits at Bank, which puts you a short ride or a long walk from Bloomsbury, Bankside and Shoreditch, so it suits all three days of this plan. The Northern and Central lines stop here, so it doesn't depend on the closed Piccadilly line.

stay.name: St Pancras London, Autograph Collection
stay.text: George Gilbert Scott's Gothic Revival hotel above St Pancras opened in 1873 as the Midland Grand. It was known until 2025 as the St Pancras Renaissance, and has since been rebranded and refurbished under Marriott's Autograph Collection. Have a drink in the Booking Office 1869, the old ticket hall, under its iron-and-glass canopy. It's a two-minute walk from Friday's breakfast and the British Library, and the Eurostar is downstairs if you're carrying on to Paris.

stay.name: The Hoxton, Holborn
stay.text: A stylish, good-value base on High Holborn with 220 soundproofed rooms, a busy lobby restaurant and bar, and breakfast cooked to order. It's a 10-minute walk from the British Museum and Lamb's Conduit Street, and close to Holborn station. The Central line runs east from Holborn toward Sunday's East End and Stratford. Rooms run small, as they do at most London hotels in this price range.

events.name: LSO with Sir Antonio Pappano: Tchaikovsky, Kendall and Liadov
events.text: If you arrive on Thursday, the London Symphony Orchestra plays Tchaikovsky's Fifth Symphony and gives the world premiere of Hannah Kendall's *I have discovered the secret of death*, with mezzo-soprano Fleur Barron. Tickets run from £18 to £75.

events.name: Imprint Art Fair
events.text: A fair of prints and editions, with galleries, publishers and artists, plus talks and live demonstrations. It's an approachable way to buy contemporary art, and runs until Sunday 1 November. Standard entry is £20.

events.name: Agatha Christie: A World of Mystery opens
events.text: Opening day of the British Library's major Christie exhibition, with more than 100 items, some never shown before. It runs until 20 June 2027.

events.name: Chelsea v Manchester United
events.text: The Premier League's lunchtime game on Halloween. If you don't have a ticket, almost any pub will show it, since it's on TNT Sports.

events.name: Maestro of the Movies: A Tribute to John Williams
events.text: The LSO plays John Williams scores from *Star Wars* to *Jaws* and *Schindler's List*, live to more than 50 minutes of film clips, presented by Edith Bowman and conducted by Anthony Gabriele.

events.name: Tottenham Hotspur v Crystal Palace
events.text: A London derby on Saturday evening, shown on Sky Sports. Because the Piccadilly line is closed, leave extra time if you're heading north from central London.

know: **Piccadilly line closed all weekend.** TfL lists no service on the entire line on Saturday 31 October and Sunday 1 November, including the Night Tube. Its list also shows Cockfosters–Uxbridge works from Wednesday 28 to Friday 30 October, so check before you rely on it on Friday. That cuts the cheap Tube route from Heathrow and affects stations like Covent Garden, Leicester Square and South Kensington. Check [TfL's planned closures](https://content.tfl.gov.uk/planned-track-closures.pdf) before you travel.

**From Heathrow (LHR):** take the Heathrow Express, a non-stop train to Paddington every 15 minutes that takes 15 minutes from Heathrow Central. Advance singles start at £10 if booked 30 or more days ahead, and under-16s ride free. Or take the Elizabeth line straight to Bond Street, Tottenham Court Road and Farringdon. On Sunday the Elizabeth line runs a reduced service at Terminal 4 and between Paddington and Maidenhead, and its trains won't stop at Acton Main Line, Hanwell or West Ealing. A black cab into the centre usually takes about an hour, more in traffic.

**From Gatwick (LGW), City (LCY), Stansted (STN) and Luton (LTN):** the Gatwick Express runs to Victoria in about 30 minutes. London City is on the DLR, about 25 minutes from Bank, but the DLR is closed between Tower Gateway and Shadwell on Sunday, so change at Bank. Stansted Express trains run to Liverpool Street, and Luton passengers take the shuttle to Luton Airport Parkway for Thameslink trains into St Pancras.

**Pay as you go:** tap a contactless card or phone, or an Oyster card, on the yellow readers when you go in and come out. Since March 2026 a zone 1 single costs £3.10 at peak and £3.00 off-peak, and daily caps are £8.90 for zones 1–2 and £16.30 for zones 1–6. Use the same card or device all day, or the cap won't apply.

**Early dark:** UK clocks went back to GMT on Sunday 25 October. Sunset is about 4:38 p.m. on Friday and 4:36 p.m. on Saturday, so plan outdoor things for the morning and keep museums for the afternoon. The forecast is mild, around 14–16°C, with sunny spells on Friday and cloud on Saturday. Pack a light waterproof anyway.

**Strikes and closures:** V&A staff are striking on 29 and 30 October. On those days V&A South Kensington is only partly open, and V&A East and its Storehouse are closed, which is why this plan visits V&A East on Sunday. No Tube strikes had been announced for this weekend when we went to press.
**Tipping:** many restaurants add a discretionary service charge of 12.5% to the bill. If it's there, you don't need to tip again. In pubs you order and pay at the bar, and nobody expects a tip.
**No fireworks this weekend:** London's big Bonfire Night displays, at Alexandra Palace, Battersea Park and Blackheath, are on 7 and 8 November, the weekend after this one.
